question: A service opens a fresh PostgreSQL connection per HTTP request. Under load, CPU on the database host is dominated by process startup and context switching, and p99 latency climbs long before disk or the planner become interesting. A developer proposes raising `max_connections` from 100 to 5000 so requests stop queueing on connection acquisition, and adds that the postmaster deserves more CPU since 'every query flows through it'. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: `max_connections` is admission control only; the real ceiling is the operating system's file-descriptor limit, so the change is harmless once `ulimit` is raised. The postmaster point stands, though — it multiplexes every client's traffic onto the backends, so it is genuinely the hot path

Every accepted connection makes the postmaster fork a full OS process that lives for the whole session, so `max_connections` bounds real processes rather than queue slots: 5000 of them multiplies per-backend memory and puts thousands of processes in contention over the same shared-memory structures, amplifying the exact symptom being profiled. And the postmaster is not on the hot path — it allocates shared memory, starts the background processes, listens and forks; after that the client talks to its own backend directly. The fix is a pooler, so a small stable set of backends serves many clients

The plan is sound in principle but incomplete: forked backends are nearly free because `fork` is copy-on-write, so the real cost is the per-connection slice of `shared_buffers`, which has to be raised in proportion to `max_connections`

Connections are not the problem — backends are recycled between sessions from an internal pool, so raising the cap changes nothing either way; the startup cost being profiled is the per-statement parse and plan work, which prepared statements would remove
explanation: The process model is the whole answer here. A running server is a family of ordinary OS processes around one block of shared memory: the postmaster allocates that memory, launches the background processes (checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher) and listens — and its only per-client job is to fork a dedicated backend, which then owns the session for its entire life and talks to the client directly. `SELECT pg_backend_pid()` names that process. So `max_connections` is not a queue depth, it is a cap on how many such processes may exist at once, and pushing it to 5000 buys 5000 processes each with its own memory, all scheduled by the OS and all contending on the shared structures (buffer table, locks, WAL buffers) that are the only place backends ever meet. That is why the standard remedy is inverted from the proposal: a connection pooler keeps the backend count small and stable while the application still opens and closes connections freely. The distractors each misplace a piece of the model — file descriptors are a real limit but not the one that makes the process expensive, and the postmaster relaying traffic is precisely the misconception the fork-per-connection design rules out; copy-on-write does make `fork` itself cheap while doing nothing about the resident cost of thousands of long-lived processes, and `shared_buffers` is shared, not divided per connection; and there is no backend reuse in core PostgreSQL — that absence is exactly the hole a pooler fills.

question: A nightly job aggregates a 16 GB table with no usable index — a plain sequential scan — and it runs while the OLTP workload is live. The team fears the scan will flush the hot OLTP pages out of shared buffers and wants to schedule downtime around it. What does the buffer manager actually do here, and where should the team's attention go?
choices: The fear is justified: replacement is clock sweep, which is strict LRU, so the scan's freshly-read pages are the most recently used and every OLTP page is evicted before the scan ends. Downtime is the only remedy
The scan cannot evict anything: pages read by a sequential scan are pinned for the duration of the scan, and pinned slots are never chosen as victims
Eviction is decided per relation — each table holds a share of the pool proportional to its size — so a 16 GB table simply owns most of the pool for the night, and the OLTP tables get what is left

A large sequential scan does not claim a fresh slot per page: it recycles a small private ring of buffers (~256 KB), so a scan of any size leaves the rest of the pool alone. And clock sweep is not LRU: it circles the pool decrementing each slot's usage count and takes the first unpinned slot at zero, so pages the OLTP workload pins repeatedly survive laps that evict pages touched once. The cache is not the problem worth downtime — the standing cost is that the job re-reads all 16 GB every night no matter how few rows the aggregate returns, which is an access-path problem, not a memory one
explanation: Every page of traffic goes through shared buffers — an array of 8 KB slots plus a hash table mapping (relation, fork, page number) to a slot — so on the face of it any big scan is a threat to the pool's contents. Two mechanisms defuse it. Clock sweep is a usage-count approximation of LRU, not LRU: each pin bumps a slot's count, the sweep decrements counts as it circles, and only an unpinned slot that has reached zero can be taken, so a page pinned repeatedly by OLTP has to survive several laps' worth of decrements before it is even eligible. On top of that, a large sequential scan is explicitly kept from claiming the pool at all — it reuses a small private ring of buffers, so the scan's page traffic churns through the same ~256 KB rather than evicting the working set. The reasoning to take away is that the cache behaves well here and the real cost is elsewhere: the job pays for the size of the table, every night, whatever the answer size. The distractors invert specific mechanics — treating clock sweep as plain LRU is what makes the eviction fear look inevitable; pinning is transient (a pin protects a slot while it is being used, and a scan that pinned 2 million pages at once could not run at all); and there is no per-relation quota in the pool, which is precisely why a ring buffer had to exist.

question: A team hides a wide join behind a view and calls it from several endpoints, each adding its own `WHERE` clause. One engineer objects that the view must compute the entire join before the endpoint's filter can apply, and wants the SQL duplicated into each endpoint instead. Another argues the opposite — that the view is faster than raw SQL because the database keeps the view's plan around. Who is right?
choices: Neither. Before any planning happens, the rewrite stage expands the view into the base tables it stands for, so the planner receives one flattened query carrying the endpoint's `WHERE` alongside the view's own — and is free to push that predicate down into the join. The view is a naming device that disappears before costing, which is also why the second claim fails: nothing is precomputed or cached, and each call is parsed, rewritten, planned and executed like any other statement (a materialized view is the different object that does store rows)

The first engineer is right: a view is planned and executed as its own unit and the caller's `WHERE` filters the result afterwards, which is why views over wide joins are a known anti-pattern. Duplicating the SQL is the standard remedy

The second engineer is right: the view's parse tree and plan are stored with the definition at `CREATE VIEW` time, so calls skip the parse and plan stages; predicate pushdown still happens, so both effects are favourable

Both effects are real and roughly cancel: the view materializes its result into a work table, and the plan cached for that materialization saves about what the extra pass costs, so the choice is stylistic
explanation: A statement crosses four stages inside the backend before any page is touched: parse (text to a parse tree), rewrite (rules apply — above all, views are expanded into the base tables they hide), plan (enumerate ways to compute the answer, cost them, keep the cheapest), execute (walk the plan tree pulling rows through it). Placing view expansion in rewrite, before the planner runs, is what settles both arguments at once. The planner never sees a view boundary to respect, so there is no wrapped result set for the caller's predicate to filter after the fact — it sees one query and can push the predicate down into the join like any other. Equally, there is no stage at which a plan could have been stored: `CREATE VIEW` records a query definition, not a plan, and every call pays parse, rewrite, plan and execute. The engineering judgement is that views are free in the way that matters and free of benefit in the way people hope for — pick them for readability and access control, not performance, and reach for a materialized view when you genuinely want stored rows. The distractors are each a coherent-sounding model of a stage that does not exist: filtering after a view is computed describes a subquery the planner failed to flatten (a real hazard with aggregates or `LIMIT` inside the view, but not the default), stored plans confuse views with prepared statements, and the 'materializes into a work table' claim invents a pass that plain views never make.

question: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on a lookup by email over a million-row table reports `Seq Scan on users`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 999999`, `Buffers: shared read=16667`, 317 ms — for a single returned row. Two fixes are proposed: add `LIMIT 1` since only one row is wanted, and raise `shared_buffers` so subsequent runs are served from cache. How should these be judged?
choices: `LIMIT 1` is the fix: the executor can stop at the first match, and since the table is walked in file order the match sits on average halfway through, so the work is halved by a one-word change

Raising `shared_buffers` is the fix: on the second run every page is a buffer hit instead of a read, and a hit is essentially free, so the 317 ms collapses to microseconds — the scan is I/O-bound and the pool is the only lever

Both are palliatives that leave the shape of the cost untouched. `LIMIT 1` does let the executor stop early — the reason a sequential scan otherwise cannot is that the last page might always hold one more match — but only when there is a match and only where it happens to sit, so a lookup for an absent email still reads all 16,667 pages: a fixed cost becomes a lottery. Caching removes the I/O but not the work: the scan still requests all 16,667 pages through the buffer manager and, per page, walks the line pointers and pays a visibility check plus filter evaluation per tuple. A sequential scan's cost tracks the size of the table, not the size of the answer; only a different access path changes that

The diagnosis is in `Rows Removed by Filter`: nearly a million rows are being run through the filter expression, so the expense is per-row expression evaluation. Rewriting the predicate — comparing a hash of the email rather than the text — removes most of the 317 ms
explanation: The executor's procedure for a filter on an unindexed column is fixed: request every page of the main fork, 0 through N−1 in file order, each through the buffer pool; per page walk the line pointers, and for each normal tuple check visibility against the query's snapshot before evaluating the `WHERE` clause; emit the survivors. Nothing in that loop is proportional to the number of rows returned, and there is no early exit — the last page might always hold one more match — which is why 16,667 pages are read for one row and would be read again next time whatever the answer. `LIMIT` is the one thing that permits stopping early, so it is not nothing, but it converts a predictable cost into a data-dependent one and does nothing at all for the miss case, which is usually the case that matters (login checks, uniqueness probes). Caching is the more seductive of the two because the numbers do improve: `shared read` becomes `shared hit` and the sequential I/O disappears. What survives is the per-page and per-tuple CPU work — buffer lookups, line-pointer walks, a million visibility checks and a million comparisons — and the requirement that the table fit in the pool at all. That gap between 'I/O removed' and 'work removed' is the whole argument for an index: the point is to turn 'look at everything' into 'read four pages', which is a change of access path, not of cache state or expression shape. The last distractor reads a real number the wrong way round: `Rows Removed by Filter` counts how many rows the scan had to examine, so it is a symptom of the access path, and a hashed comparison would still examine every one of them.

question: After an unclean shutdown, an ops engineer notices that the mtime on a busy table's data file is hours old even though transactions were committing seconds before the crash. Separately, the team wants lower commit latency on this write-heavy workload, and he proposes running the checkpointer far more frequently so that 'commits have less to lose'. Assess both halves.
choices: The stale mtime is the bug: a commit has to flush the pages it modified, so an hours-old data file means fsyncs are being lost somewhere in the storage stack — and more frequent checkpoints are the right mitigation until that is fixed

The mtime is expected, and more frequent checkpoints genuinely do cut commit latency: a commit cannot return until the WAL segment it wrote into has been folded into a checkpoint, so shorter checkpoint intervals shorten that wait

The mtime is expected, but the durability reasoning is inverted: the write-ahead rule requires the modified page to reach the data file before its log record counts as durable, which is what makes commit expensive; checkpointing more often is precisely what makes each commit's flush cheaper

The stale mtime is what the design predicts and costs nothing: an `INSERT` finds room via the free space map, writes the tuple into a pinned buffer and marks it dirty — the data file is untouched then and at commit. A commit flushes only the WAL, one sequential write, and the dirty pages reach disk later via the background writer and checkpointer, because the write-ahead rule (a change may reach the data files only after the record describing it is on disk) makes them redoable from the log. Frequent checkpoints therefore do nothing for commit latency, which is the WAL fsync; they add page writes and make a write-heavy workload worse. Their real lever is recovery time, since replay starts at the last checkpoint — and the commit-latency lever is the fsync itself, which can commit many concurrent transactions in one flush
explanation: The write path and the WAL contract only make sense together. Writing a row is entirely a memory operation: ask the free space map for a page with room (or extend the file), pin it in the pool, place the tuple and its line pointer, mark the buffer dirty — an `UPDATE` adds a complete new version plus an `xmax` stamp on the old one, a `DELETE` is the stamp alone. The data file is not touched, not then and not at commit, so a data file hours older than the last commit is the expected steady state rather than a symptom. What makes that safe is the rule that names the log: a change may reach the data files only after the record describing it is safely on disk. From that rule the economy follows — commit flushes the WAL only, one sequential write, and everything the crash takes from memory is redone from the log on restart, replaying forward from the last checkpoint. Both halves of the proposal fail against that picture. Commit latency is the cost of a WAL fsync, which no checkpoint schedule touches; what does touch it is that a single fsync can commit many concurrent transactions at once, so batching and concurrency are the levers. And checkpoints are pure additional page writes: they exist to bound how much log a crash would have to replay, which makes their frequency a trade of recovery time against write amplification — exactly the wrong knob to turn toward on a write-heavy system. The remaining distractors invert the ordering rule itself (page before log rather than log before page), which would abolish the entire reason the log is called write-ahead, or read a normal deferred write as lost fsyncs.
